artifacts.summary: Confirms the sort/comm collation-split defect via live reproduction, resolves whether pinning the producer sort alone suffices (empirically yes here, but comm-site pinning recommended too for defense-in-depth), audits all 5 sort/comm sites in the script, and lays out the fix, test-fixture, and deploy recommendations for the planner.

memory_candidates.content: GNU comm's own 'input is not in sorted order' check is evaluated under whatever locale comm itself runs in at invocation time, independent of which locale produced the file. Two files sorted under different collations will each be flagged as 'unsorted' by comm regardless of which locale comm runs under; two files sorted under the SAME collation as each other (even if that shared collation differs from comm's own ambient locale) compare cleanly with no warning, because comm's streaming merge only needs the two inputs to agree with each other, not with some absolute notion of sortedness. Practical implication: when a shell pipeline's sort output is cross-tool compared (via comm/diff/join) against another tool's sort output, pinning ONE producer to a shared collation (e.g. LC_ALL=C to match Python's sorted()) is often sufficient by itself, but pinning the comparison site too is the safer, edit-resistant choice.

glibc's en_US.UTF-8 dictionary collation treats underscore (_) as a very low-weight/near-ignorable character relative to letters, while C/byte-order collation places '_' (0x5F) after all uppercase letters (0x41-0x5A) and before lowercase letters (0x61-0x7A). Any identifier pair combining snake_case and camelCase segments sharing a common prefix up to the case/underscore divergence point (e.g. hn_stab vs hnStabMirror) sorts in a different relative order under the two collations. This is the concrete trigger condition for locale-dependent sort/comm bugs comparing identifier lists.
